The electrostatic field invisibility cloak (EFIC) can perfectly hide two-dimensional objects without disturbing external electrostatic fields.
The bilayer cloak consists of an inner perfect electric conductor (steel) layer and an outer air layer embedded in castor oil.
The dielectric constant of castor oil used as background medium is 4.3.
The radii ratio for the bilayer cloak outer to inner layer is approximately 1.3 (c/b = 1.3).
The inner radius of the steel layer is 1.3 cm, outer radius 1.5 cm; the air layer extends to 1.95 cm outer radius.
Numerical simulations show that the bilayer cloak guides the electric field around the cloaked region without distortion.
Experimental measurements of the electric field near the cloak agree well with simulations, validating the cloak's performance.
The carpet cloak uses transformation optics to design a cloak that hides a PEC bump on a grounded plane.
The carpet cloak requires anisotropic dielectric constants, realized by multilayer metamaterials composed of air and ultrapure water.
The filling ratio of air in the carpet cloak metamaterial is about 88%.
The cloak designs rely on solving the 2D Laplace equation for electrostatic potential with boundary conditions ensuring continuity of potential and displacement.
The bilayer cloak is scalable and can be extended to micro-nanoscale and three-dimensional configurations.
The bilayer cloak only works effectively for uniform or inhomogeneous electrostatic fields, not for point sources.
The wavelength for static fields is infinite, eliminating subwavelength design constraints present in wave cloaks.
The electrostatic measurement instrument uses a field-effect transistor probe with high input resistance to detect local electrostatic fields.
Transformation optics for the carpet cloak involves a coordinate transformation stretching a triangular region to hide the bump.
The dielectric tensor components for the carpet cloak are derived analytically and depend on geometric parameters α and β.
The bilayer cloak's inner layer uses materials with effectively infinite dielectric constant (PEC), differing from magnetic or thermal cloaks where inner layers have zero parameters.
The cloak can be used to manipulate electrostatic fields in applications such as shielding, detection, and field control.
The study demonstrates both theoretical and experimental validation of electrostatic cloaking using naturally available materials.
